q: Which is a common cause of road accidents?
right: Overspeeding
why: Higher speed leaves less time to react.

q: What should you do before starting a journey?
right: Check your vehicle and plan your trip
wrong: Skip the checks to save time
why: A quick check of brakes, tyres and lights prevents breakdowns.

q: Why should you keep a safe distance from the vehicle ahead?
right: To have time to stop if it brakes
wrong: To look at its number plate
why: A gap gives you time and space to react.

q: What is the safest way to deal with tiredness on a long drive?
right: Stop at a safe place and rest
wrong: Open the window and keep going
why: Only rest cures tiredness. Fatigue slows your reactions.

q: Who must follow traffic rules?
right: Everyone using the road
why: Rules apply to all road users.

q: Is it safe to use a mobile phone while riding a two-wheeler?
right: No, never
wrong: Yes, if the road is empty
why: Phones take your eyes and hands away from controlling the vehicle.

q: Why should you use your indicator?
right: To tell others you plan to turn or change lane
wrong: It is needed only at night
why: Indicators let others predict your move.

q: When is it safe to overtake?
right: When the road ahead is clearly free and visible
wrong: Near the top of a hill
why: Overtaking needs a clear view. Never overtake on bends, crests or crossings.

q: When should a two-wheeler rider wear a helmet?
right: On every ride
why: Crashes happen on short trips as well.

q: Who should wear a seatbelt in a car?
right: Everyone in the car
why: Rear passengers can be thrown forward without a belt.

q: Why must the helmet chin strap be fastened?
right: An open strap lets the helmet come off in a crash
why: A helmet only protects if it stays on your head.

q: Do airbags replace seatbelts?
right: No, they work together with seatbelts
wrong: Yes, but only in new cars
why: Airbags are designed to work together with seatbelts.

q: Where should the lap part of a seatbelt sit?
right: Low across the hips
why: A low, snug lap belt protects the strong hip bones.

q: Where is the safest place to cross the road?
right: At a zebra crossing
why: Drivers expect people at crossings.

q: What do you do first before crossing?
right: Stop and look for vehicles in both directions
why: Look right, left, then right again.

q: A school bus has stopped. What should children do?
right: Wait for it to stop fully and cross only when safe
wrong: Cross right in front of it
why: Drivers cannot see people close behind or in front of a bus.

q: How can you stay visible while walking at night?
right: Wear light or reflective clothes
wrong: Walk in the middle of the road
why: Reflective items help drivers notice you earlier.

q: What does a red traffic light mean?
right: Stop
why: Stop behind the stop line.

q: What shape are mandatory signs usually?
right: Circular with a red ring
why: Mandatory signs are mostly circular with a red border.

q: What does a yellow light tell you?
right: Get ready to stop
why: Yellow is a warning that red is coming.

q: A traffic police officer signals you to stop while the light is green. What do you do?
right: Obey the officer and stop
why: Directions from a traffic police officer overrule the signal.

q: Which number do you call for emergency help in India?
why: 112 is the national emergency number.

q: What should you do if you see an accident?
right: Stay safe, call 112 and give the exact location
why: Safety and a quick call for help come first.

q: Should you move a seriously injured person?
right: Not unless there is immediate danger such as fire
wrong: Yes, lift them into a car at once
why: Moving a badly hurt person can make injuries worse. Wait for trained responders.

q: Which headlights should you use for normal night driving?
right: Dipped (low-beam) headlights
why: Dipped headlights light the road without dazzling other drivers.

q: What should you do with your speed at night?
right: Slow down, because you see less far
wrong: Speed up, the roads are empty
Keep the same speed as the day
why: Darkness shortens how far you can see, so you need more time to react.

q: What is a good habit when you walk near a road at night?
right: Wear bright or reflective clothes
wrong: Walk in the middle of the road
why: Bright or reflective items help drivers notice you earlier.

q: What does a closed railway barrier mean?
right: Stop and wait until it opens fully
wrong: Go around it if no train is visible
why: A train cannot stop quickly. Never cross when the barrier is down.

q: Why should you avoid sudden braking on a wet road?
right: The vehicle can skid
why: Wet roads give less grip, so brake early and gently.

q: What is the safest way to drive in fog?
right: Slow down, use low beams and keep a bigger gap
wrong: Use high beams to see further
Drive faster to leave the fog sooner
why: High beams reflect off fog. Low speed and low beams give you time and visibility.

q: Where should you park?
right: In a marked bay or where parking is allowed
why: Crossings, footpaths and bends must stay clear for walkers and for visibility.

q: What should you do near a school?
right: Slow down and watch for children
wrong: Park on the crossing to drop children
why: Children can step out suddenly. Be ready to stop.

q: How often should you take a break on a long highway trip?
right: About every two hours, or sooner if tired
wrong: Only when the fuel runs out
why: Regular rests keep you alert and cut the risk of tired-driving crashes.

q: What should you do if the fog is too thick to drive safely?
right: Stop at a safe place well away from the road
wrong: Stop in the middle of the lane
Follow the tail lights very closely
why: Never stop on the carriageway. Move off the road and wait.

q: Which number can you call for help on a national highway?
why: 1033 is the National Highway helpline. For emergencies you can also call 112.

q: Why must you never go around a lowered railway barrier?
right: A train cannot stop quickly
why: Trains need a long distance to stop, so the risk is far too high.

q: What should you do before helping a person who is blind to cross?
right: Ask if they would like help
why: Always ask first, then follow what the person tells you they need.

q: Who benefits from a pedestrian ramp?
right: Wheelchair users, prams and walkers
why: Ramps give a smooth way up and down the kerb.

q: How should drivers treat people who cross slowly?
right: Wait patiently and give them time
why: Some people need more time to cross, and that is fine.

q: What is tactile paving?
right: Raised patterns on the ground that guide people with low vision
wrong: A kind of road paint for cars
why: The raised bumps and lines can be felt with the feet or a cane.

q: What do audio pedestrian signals do?
right: Make a sound to say when it is safe to cross
why: The sound helps people who cannot see the signal.

q: Why should you not park on a footpath?
right: It blocks people, including wheelchair users and people with low vision
wrong: It is better for the footpath
It saves the road space for walkers
why: Footpaths must stay clear so everyone can pass safely.

q: If you offer your arm to a person who is blind, what is right?
right: Do it only if they want it, and let them hold your arm
wrong: Grab their hand and lead them
why: Let the person choose how to be guided. Never grab or pull.

q: What should you do with tactile paving?
right: Keep it clear of vehicles and goods
why: Blocking it can leave a person with low vision without a safe path.

q: Why are vehicle blind spots dangerous for walkers?
right: The driver cannot see you when you are very close to a large vehicle
wrong: Blind spots only exist on bikes
why: Stay clear of the front, back and sides of big vehicles.

q: You reach a railway crossing and the barrier is up. What should you do?
right: Look and listen both ways, then cross if it is clear
wrong: Stop on the tracks to check
why: Barriers can go down quickly. Stay alert and never stop on the tracks.

q: A green walking signal turns on. What is the safest next step?
right: Check that vehicles have stopped, then cross
why: The signal helps, but always check that vehicles have really stopped.

q: What does a stop line on the road tell you?
right: Where to stop when the signal is red
wrong: The start of a school zone
why: Stop behind the line so walkers can use the crossing.

q: What does a solid line along the centre of the road usually mean?
right: Do not cross it or overtake
why: A solid line warns that overtaking is not safe or not allowed there.

q: Which sign shape usually means “be careful”?
right: A triangle with a red border
why: Cautionary signs are generally triangles with a red border.

q: What does a blue rectangular sign usually give?
right: Helpful information, such as a hospital or parking
why: Informatory signs are mostly blue rectangles.

q: Why is wrong-side driving dangerous?
right: Vehicles coming the other way have little time to avoid you
wrong: It is safe on empty roads
why: Head-on crashes are very serious. Always drive on your own side.

q: Which action best reduces the risk of a crash?
right: Keep a safe speed and distance, and stay alert
wrong: Use a phone at red lights only
why: Most crashes can be avoided by safe habits, not by luck or safety gear alone.

q: Why is triple riding on a two-wheeler unsafe?
right: The rider loses balance and control
why: Two-wheelers are made for the rider and one pillion at most.

q: What should a cyclist use after dark?
right: Lights and reflectors
why: Lights and reflectors help drivers see you.

q: What is the best way to check a helmet fits?
right: It sits level and snug, and does not move around
wrong: It should be loose and wobbly
It can sit on the back of the head
why: A snug, level helmet with a fastened strap protects best.

q: Should a helmet be replaced after a hard impact?
right: Yes, because it may be damaged inside
why: A hard hit can weaken the helmet even when it looks fine.

q: What information should you give when you call 112?
right: The exact location and what has happened
why: Clear location and details help responders reach the place fast.

q: Where should you stand when you stop to help at a crash?
right: In a safe place away from traffic
wrong: In the middle of the road
why: Your own safety comes first.
